title: Tagging the Neurons Behind an Experience
endLine: Tag active neurons genetically, then switch them to test their role.

scenes.tts: How do you catch the exact neurons active during one experience? During that moment, a linked group of cells fires together, then fades back. Watching them fire only gives correlation, the lowest rung of evidence. It shows those cells carry information, not whether they drive behaviour.
scenes.caption: How do you catch the exact neurons active during one experience? During that moment, a linked group of cells fires together, then fades back. scenes.visual: Full-frame schematic neural field (labelled 'schematic') of muted slate-blue neurons with faint branching links drifting gently. An 'Experience' pulse sweeps across the top banner; a small scattered group of neurons lights up amber with glowing links, then fades back into the dark crowd. A bottom rung labelled 'Correlation' rises on the left beside a faint question mark over an unlabelled behaviour arrow.

scenes.visual: The same schematic neural field continues drifting gently; the title 'Tagging the Neurons Behind an Experience' fades in cleanly at centre in high-contrast text and clears.

scenes.tts: To move past correlation, activity-dependent genetic tagging labels cells as they fire. During a chosen experience, a specific group of neurons becomes active together. A driver switched on by the firing itself gives those active cells a lasting genetic label. Quiet neighbours stay untagged, so the active group stays marked after firing ends.
scenes.caption: To move past correlation, activity-dependent genetic tagging labels cells as they fire. During a chosen experience, a specific group of neurons becomes active together. A driver switched on by the firing itself gives those active cells a lasting genetic label. Quiet neighbours stay untagged, so the active group stays marked after firing ends.
scenes.visual: Carried schematic neural field. An 'Experience' window opens at top and the same scattered group lights up amber. A 'Genetic tag' ring locks in bright cyan around only the amber firing cells while quiet neighbours remain slate-blue. The experience ends and amber activity fades, yet the bright cyan genetic tags stay glowing on that exact group.
scenes.narration: To move past correlation, activity-dependent genetic tagging labels cells as they fire. During a chosen experience, a specific group of neurons becomes active together. A driver switched on by the firing itself gives those active cells a lasting genetic label. Quiet neighbours stay untagged, so the active group stays marked after firing ends.

scenes.tts: That lasting genetic tag lets you switch those exact cells on or off later. Now you can climb above correlation to two direct interventions. Turning tagged cells back on tests sufficiency: are they enough to drive the behaviour? Turning them off while the animal remembers by itself tests necessity.
scenes.caption: That lasting genetic tag lets you switch those exact cells on or off later. Now you can climb above correlation to two direct interventions. Turning tagged cells back on tests sufficiency: are they enough to drive the behaviour? Turning them off while the animal remembers by itself tests necessity.
scenes.visual: Same carried schematic network with cyan-tagged cells glowing. 'ON' and 'OFF' switches appear on the right and two upper rungs ('Sufficiency' and 'Necessity') grow above 'Correlation' on the left. First, the 'ON' switch flips without an experience: only the cyan-tagged cells light up amber and push a schematic 'Behaviour' meter upward ('Sufficiency' highlights). Next, a recall cue arrives while the 'OFF' switch dims the cyan-tagged cells and the 'Behaviour' meter drops ('Necessity' highlights).
scenes.narration: That lasting genetic tag lets you switch those exact cells on or off later. Now you can climb above correlation to two direct interventions. Turning tagged cells back on tests sufficiency: are they enough to drive the behaviour? Turning them off while the animal remembers by itself tests necessity.

scenes.tts: Test the necessity switch. Suppose you tag cells active during learning, then turn them off while the animal remembers by itself. Recall fails. Does that prove the memory was erased, or only something narrower?
scenes.caption: Test the necessity switch. Suppose you tag cells active during learning, then turn them off while the animal remembers by itself. Recall fails. Does that prove the memory was erased, or only something narrower?
scenes.visual: Same schematic network held with the 'OFF' switch active: a cue pulse enters, the cyan-tagged cells stay silenced, and the schematic 'Behaviour' meter falls flat. A high-contrast question card settles in the upper frame: 'Recall failed. Was the memory erased?'
scenes.narration: Test the necessity switch. Suppose you tag cells active during learning, then turn them off while the animal remembers by itself. Recall fails. Does that prove the memory was erased, or only something narrower?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. The question card 'Recall failed. Was the memory erased?' stays on screen while the silenced cyan-tagged cells pulse gently in the schematic network below and a thin progress bar advances smoothly across the bottom.

scenes.tts: Impaired recall does not prove the memory was erased. It shows the animal uses those tagged cells at that moment. Sufficiency and necessity answer different questions, so neither intervention alone locates a memory. Every rung of the ladder needs its own controls. Networks also share cells across memories, and circuits reorganize over days.

scenes.visual: The question card resolves to 'Not erased: used at that moment' as the 'OFF' switch releases and the cyan-tagged cells brighten again. On the left ladder, a 'Controls' check appears beside each rung ('Correlation', 'Sufficiency', 'Necessity'). In the schematic network, a second memory group glows violet and shares several cells with the cyan group; then a 'Days' scrubber glides forward as strengthened links gradually shift to neighbouring cells (schematic consolidation).

scenes.tts: In gut-brain sensing, Tan and colleagues used the activity-dependent driver TRAP two. It tagged neurons of the caudal nucleus of the solitary tract that responded to sugar reaching the gut. In six animals, silencing their transmitter release abolished development of sugar preference. Innate attraction to sugar or sweeteners stayed. That separated first-sip attraction from learning, leaving the intestinal cell type open.
scenes.caption: In gut-brain sensing, Tan and colleagues used the activity-dependent driver TRAP2. Innate attraction to sugar or sweeteners stayed. That separated first-sip attraction from learning, leaving the intestinal cell type open.
scenes.visual: The carried schematic neural field morphs smoothly into a schematic gut-to-brain pathway labelled 'Solitary tract (schematic)' receiving a sugar signal from a schematic gut tube below. A 'TRAP2 (n = 6)' tag locks cyan onto the sugar-activated neurons. Flipping the 'OFF' switch silences transmitter release: a schematic 'Learned preference' bar drops flat while a schematic 'Innate attraction' bar stays high, and a question mark marks the gut wall for the open intestinal cell type.

scenes.tts: In the gut, the same trick solved a rarity problem. Enterochromaffin cells make more than ninety percent of the body's serotonin. Yet they are under one percent of intestinal epithelial cells. Finding so few cells had blocked single-cell work. In 2017, Bellono and colleagues genetically tagged them in cultured mouse mini-intestines, then checked native tissue.

scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly into the schematic gut wall from the prior scene, showing a dense row of pale schematic epithelial cells with very rare enterochromaffin cells among them. Two proportional bars drawn from the stated figures display '>90% serotonin' beside '<1% epithelial cells'. A bright genetic tag lights up the rare enterochromaffin cells inside a schematic cultured mini-intestine and then in schematic native tissue, labelled 'Bellono and colleagues, 2017'.

scenes.tts: In memory circuits, learning strengthens links among cells active together, forming a linked group. On this model, a close enough cue pulls the rest of that group back on. That is one proposed way recall could work, not a definition of remembering. Engram experiments tag those active members to test sufficiency and necessity directly.

scenes.visual: Smooth return to the original carried schematic neural field. Links thicken between the active group during learning. A partial cue lights up a fragment of the group, and pulses race across the strengthened links to pull the remaining members back on (schematic pattern completion). Cyan engram tags lock onto the group as the 'ON' (Sufficiency) and 'OFF' (Necessity) switches highlight.

scenes.tts: Activity fades in moments, and watching alone stops at correlation. A lasting genetic tag preserves the exact cells active during an experience. Switching them on or off then tests what role they actually play.
